title: Better, Saner Homework, Pt 1: 6 Tips to Make It More Doable for Us
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart explains why he assigns homework to ninth graders, as an opportunity and as a way to increase the volume of reading, writing, and argument beyond a sixty-minute class. His central claim is that homework must be doable for students, parents, and teachers alike, and this first installment focuses on the teacher's side. He offers six tips: limit homework to a few go-to types, explicitly teach each type, lean on the five key beliefs rather than grades or prizes, keep the system sensible to families, make grading proportionate, and accept that perfect completion is rare. The move throughout is to treat teacher sustainability as a design constraint on homework rather than an afterthought. Concrete examples include articles of the week graded in seconds, and low-stakes quizzes in place of grading content review.
points: Stuart gives homework for two stated reasons, as an opportunity to learn beyond the school day and as a way to add reading, writing, and argument volume that class time cannot hold.
Limiting homework to a few recurring types makes it feasible to teach each type's moves thoroughly in class.
He argues the five key beliefs (credibility, belonging, effort, efficacy, value) motivate homework completion more durably than grades, guilt, or prizes, and spare teachers from micromanaging.
Grading must be proportionate to purpose: article-of-the-week responses get four to five seconds, and content review is checked through frequent low-stakes quizzes instead.
A one-page explanation of what students do and why replaces the long syllabus for parents.
quotes: I want the Stuart children to have opportunities to learn beyond the school day, and so I want to give that same opportunity to my students. I explain this to my students, that one sign of my love for them is that I give them homework.

Here's the first big idea: homework has got to be doable for all parties: students, parents/guardians, and teachers. My students have to understand what I expect, why I've assigned the work, why it's worth their time.

If kids don't get how to do what we've asked them, they'll be less likely to do it. If parents can't keep straight what their kids are expected to do and why they're expected to do it, they'll be less able to create conditions at home that are amenable to homework.

Explicitly teach students how to do everything they're expected to do for each homework type. This is why it's so helpful to limit the types of homework you assign: each type needs lots of clear, in-class instruction and practice.

To help my students cultivate the motivation to do work at home, then, I target the key beliefs. And this is not just because the beliefs drive behavior more enduringly than external motivators (e.g., grades, prizes) — it's because I'm trying to make my job doable. If I have to micromanage homework completion, I'm going to go crazy, I'm going to bring work home, and I'm going to build an unbalanced life.

And finally, remember: there aren't any silver bullets, and 100% homework completion rates are rare. Teaching isn't about achieving perfection — it's striving, constantly, toward the long-term flourishing of kids (and, if you're like me, doing that in a way that's sustainable, that makes it feasible to keep teaching for decades, getting 5-10% better at the work each year).
